items.objective_and_difficulty: Clear level-2 application of singular head-noun agreement despite the plural noun in the of-phrase.
items.notes: Box is the singular subject, so was shared agrees. The plural auxiliaries in A-C do not. The three wrong forms differ in tense or aspect, though all rely on the same agreement error.

items.notes: 7/3-2/5=29/15, then multiplying by 15 gives 29. All four numeric answers are different.

items.objective_and_difficulty: Pronoun clarity is on topic and approximately level 2, but the stated selection criterion does not uniquely select a revision.
items.notes: D explicitly says the actor was nervous and preserves the added fact. B explicitly says the director was nervous. Both B and D remove ambiguous pronoun reference; the question asks only which revision makes reference unambiguous, without explicitly requiring preservation of the actor fact. If preserving the fact is an implicit requirement, D is the intended best answer, but a literal reading admits B.

items.notes: 3/4 times 8/9 is 24/36 = 2/3. All alternatives are numerically distinct.

items.notes: 3/4+5/6=19/12, and 8 times 19/12 is 38/3. All alternatives are numerically distinct.

items.objective_and_difficulty: Level-2 explicit bounded integer condition; all values are in the stated domain.

items.objective_and_difficulty: Tests pronoun clarity at roughly level 2, but the apparent clear sentence has no pronoun to reference.
items.notes: A names Lucas twice and is clear, but it has no pronoun, so it does not literally have an unambiguous pronoun reference. B allows they to mean Lucas, Ben, or both; D leaves he between Lucas and Ben; C begins with he without an established antecedent. The stem needs to ask which revision avoids ambiguous reference or provide a candidate with a pronoun and a single established antecedent.

items.objective_and_difficulty: Collective-noun agreement is on topic and level 2, but the stem does not specify a dialect or whether committee is treated as a unit or its members.
items.notes: B has approved is standard singular agreement in American usage. Plural committee with have approved, are approving, or were approving is accepted in some English varieties and can express member-focused agreement. Without a stated convention or context, the offered choices cannot be graded as one unqualified correct completion. Tense/aspect is also unspecified.
